key_findings: REA bridges engines in four shapes behind one AnalysisClient seam: scripts injected into a host app that open a local socket (Hopper Python, Ghidra HeadlessScript, Cutter plugin), owned one-shot child processes (Kuna), owned REPL processes (GDB/MI, Rizin), and adapters over third-party MCP servers REA never launches (IDA, JEB) (src/application/AnalysisProvider.ts L168-199, L287-300; docs/architecture.mermaid).

In-app bridges share one protocol shape: private runtime dir -> random 32-byte token + run_id written to a 0600 file (bootstrap.py or session.json, never argv/env) -> script binds a user-only Unix socket or 127.0.0.1:0 -> REA polls the endpoint under one absolute deadline -> health/ping must echo run_id before any operation (src/hopper/HopperClient.ts L468-583; bridge/ghidra/ReaGhidraBridge.java L190-254, L268-316; SECURITY.md L31-32).

Every request line carries the bearer token compared in constant time, request objects must have exactly the expected key set, and responses are validated with strict zod schemas; auth-failure text is replaced with a fixed string (bridge/hopper_bridge.py L1340-1354, L1429-1440; ReaGhidraBridge.java L4974-5007, L5097-5102; src/hopper/protocol.ts; src/ghidra/protocol.ts).

Process ownership is proven, not assumed: REA_PROCESS_RUN_ID is injected into the child env, the child is spawned detached into its own process group, and cleanup refuses to SIGKILL a group unless every live member's token matches, with /proc/<pid>/stat start-time identity read before and after the token read to defeat PID reuse (src/process/ProviderProcess.ts L254-341; src/process/ProcessOwnership.ts L372-512, L225-240; src/process/ProcessOwnershipObservation.ts L1221-1279, L1489-1493).

Stop is fail-closed and retryable: ProviderProcessSupervisor.stop runs token-verified cleanup first, else SIGTERM (250 ms) -> SIGKILL (1000 ms) -> status 'incomplete', which resets the shared stop promise, retains ownership in a ProcessOwnershipEvidenceOwner ledger, and surfaces to MCP as recovery.kind=retry_cleanup on the next close_binary (src/process/ProviderProcess.ts L637-646, L710-769; src/providers/OwnedCommandCleanup.ts; docs/mcp-contracts.md L1005-1017).

Windows implements the same contract via a package-owned Node-API addon: suspended child atomically assigned to a kill-on-close Job Object with breakaway disabled, protected DACL (current user + SYSTEM) on a private NTFS runtime, handle-based cleanup retried only on Win32 codes 32/33 (10 x 100 ms), and a loader that checks version/ABI/Node-API/PE machine/SHA-256 before granting authority; a requested control the artifact lacks refuses the launch (native/windows/README.md; src/windows/WindowsNativeLoader.ts L32-71; src/windows/WindowsOwnedProcess.ts L14-19, L117-125; src/windows/WindowsPrivateRuntime.ts L57-58).

Deadlines are one absolute monotonic ProviderStartupDeadline composed with the caller AbortSignal, classifying 'cancelled' vs 'timeout' and passing remainingMs into each phase; Ghidra's 330 s default covers import+analysis+bridge+handshake lazily on the first query, Hopper's is 120 s, both overridable at launch and Ghidra's also at runtime (src/process/ProviderDeadline.ts L31-158; src/domain/analysisResourceLimits.ts L29-32; docs/installation.md L1268-1294).

Output and payloads are bounded at every layer: readline(limit+1) on the bridge, REA_BRIDGE_MAX_REQUEST_BYTES 7464..536870887 (default 16 MiB) measured before allocation on both sides, head/tail BoundedOutputExcerpt, LF-frame byte caps, per-stream retention budgets, 64 KiB late-output cap after stop (bridge/hopper_bridge.py L18-31, L1318-1331; src/process/BoundedOutputExcerpt.ts; src/process/BoundedControlLines.ts; src/process/ProviderProcess.ts L29).

Private runtime roots redirect all engine state: Ghidra gets HOME/TMPDIR/XDG_*/APPDATA/LOCALAPPDATA and -Duser.home/-Djava.io.tmpdir inside the root, inherited _JAVA_OPTIONS/JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS/JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS are cleared, the project is -readOnly -deleteProject, and the bridge script is selected by explicit path so cwd cannot shadow it (src/ghidra/GhidraLauncher.ts L913-1066, L1069-1176; docs/installation.md L1584-1596; docs/windows-ghidra-p0.md L53-55).

Leases die with their owner: acquireOwnedLease uses a listening Unix socket (or \\.\pipe\rea-lease-<key>) whose owner replies {runId, processId}; ECONNREFUSED means stale and is recovered under a .recovery mkdir mutex; the lease directory is opened O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW and chmod'd on the fd (src/process/OwnedLease.ts L80-195, L305-344; src/process/HopperLease.ts L17-50).

The Cutter plugin shows how to bridge a host that requires UI-thread execution: a QObject dispatcher with Signal.emit + threading.Event, a document_generation counter every command must match, up to 64 completion receipts so a later CLI can prove whether a timed-out command ran, HMAC challenge/response (rea-auth-v2) with signed response frames, 8 max connection workers, and a UI timeout that poisons the session until restart (bridge/cutter/rea_bridge.py L461-592, L612-682, L737-808).

IDA adaptation enforces a read-only rule over someone else's engine: tools/list is checked against a pinned profile and fails closed listing missing names; attached mode binds target identity by SHA-256 of the original input plus image base and never saves/closes the GUI database; headless mode copies input into a private workspace, opens with mode force_headless, closes with save:false and verifies absence via idb_list; URLs must be literal loopback with redirects refused and inherited env suppressed (docs/ida-provider.md L9, L54-56, L175; src/ida/IdaSessionClient.ts L702-704, L923-945; src/ida/IdaMcpConnection.ts L479-507; src/ida/IdaConfiguration.ts L66-71).

Capability descriptors carry explicit per-operation effects (mutatesArtifact, launchesProcess, mayShowUi, mayAccessNetwork, mayWriteFilesystem, changesPermissions, requiresRoot) plus limitations and retryable availability; IDA GUI-proxy operations advertise may_show_ui: true (src/application/AnalysisProvider.ts L242-287; docs/ida-provider.md L149).

REA already contains a minimal GUI-driving precedent without a scripting API: scripts/hopper-demo-x11.py runs Hopper on a private Xvfb display, enumerates X windows by title via ctypes Xlib, clicks a dialog-relative point with XTest, binds its lifetime to the owner's stdin pipe, and verifies the Hopper process is its descendant via /proc/<pid>/exe with enumerated failure exit codes (scripts/hopper-demo-x11.py L22-40, L226-297, L365-432).

REA's docs state none of this is a sandbox: same-user processes are trusted, engines parse untrusted input with the user's authority, GDB/Rizin consoles and Frida scripts are unrestricted, and abrupt owner death can leave private files or orphan upstream IDA workers (SECURITY.md L33-36; docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md L43, L86; docs/frida-instrumentation.md L20; docs/windows-ghidra-p0.md L238-239; docs/ida-provider.md L188).
extensibility_points: Single AnalysisProvider/AnalysisClient seam (execute/close/executeIfReady + CapabilityDescriptor with effects and limitations) so a new engine is one provider module plus a bridge or MCP adapter wired in src/composition (src/application/AnalysisProvider.ts L139-300).

Transport-agnostic session descriptor: the Ghidra bridge switches between unix-socket and authenticated-loopback-tcp from one JSON descriptor, mirrored by GhidraTransportKind on the client (ReaGhidraBridge.java L256-266; src/ghidra/GhidraTransport.ts L25).

Reusable bridge-side script template shared by Hopper/Ghidra/Cutter: private descriptor -> private listener -> per-frame token check -> closed method table -> fixed error-type enum -> health/ping echoing run_id -> progress/diagnostic events.

ProcessOwnershipHost is a narrow OS seam (listProcesses, environment, runTokens, processIdentities, captureBaseline, signalGroup) so new platforms implement observation while cleanup policy stays shared (src/process/ProcessOwnership.ts L181-208).

ProviderStartupDeadline is a single deadline object threaded through spawn, endpoint discovery, connect, handshake and requests; JebMcpDeadline/KunaDeadline wrap it for SDK-specific abort identities (src/process/ProviderDeadline.ts; src/jeb/JebMcpDeadline.ts).

Typed retryable cleanup chain: ProviderProcessStopResult.incomplete -> ProviderCleanupError -> AnalysisCleanupLease retained on RetainedResourceScope -> MCP recovery.kind=retry_cleanup (src/providers/OwnedCommandCleanup.ts; docs/mcp-contracts.md L1005-1017).

SharedStartupAttempt + DeferredAnalysisClient give lazy, shared, individually-cancellable startup where only the last departing waiter cancels the producer and close joins it (src/process/SharedStartupAttempt.ts L66-78; src/providers/AnalysisClientCreation.ts).
Runtime settings as immutable revisions with a declared enforcement owner per setting, captured per accepted operation via AsyncLocalStorage (docs/design/limits-and-recovery.md).

Capability discovery before use: IDA tools/list profile check, JEB live catalog probe, Hopper/Ghidra health capability arrays and read_only flag, Windows loader self-test; missing controls produce RuntimeControlUnavailableError projected as a typed capability refusal with remediation (src/process/RuntimeControlUnavailableError.ts L30-43; src/windows/WindowsOwnedProcess.ts L54-71).

Bounded-output primitives (BoundedOutputExcerpt, readBoundedControlLines, boundedUtf8Text, ProcessDiagnosticBudget) and OwnedFileHandle/OwnedStagedOutput close-state machines are standalone and reusable (src/process/*.ts; src/filesystem/*.ts).
relevance_to_control_plane: Borrow the 'wrap an external tool safely' checklist verbatim: private runtime root per session, secrets via 0600 descriptor consumed once, random token + run_id with constant-time compare and run_id echo on handshake, exact-key request validation and strict response schemas, payload ceilings measured before allocation, one absolute startup deadline with cancelled/timeout classification, run-token + start-time ownership proof before any signal, fail-closed retryable stop.

The Hopper/Cutter bridges are the exact pattern for driving a GUI app that has a scripting API: a script loaded through the app's own plugin/script flag opens an authenticated local socket, binds to one document identity, translates a closed method table onto the app API, and marshals onto the UI thread with a hang detector that poisons the session instead of blocking.

scripts/hopper-demo-x11.py is a seed for driving apps without a scripting API (private display, window enumeration, synthetic input, ownership check via /proc/<pid>/exe, enumerated failure codes); generalize to accessibility-tree-first (AT-SPI/UIA/AX) with synthetic input as fallback while keeping the same ownership and deadline discipline.

Reuse CapabilityDescriptor.effects as the tool-registry schema and extend it for drive operations (sendsInput, readsScreen, persistsState, destructive) so MCP clients can gate side-effecting tools; REA already marks GUI-moving IDA ops may_show_ui: true.

Adopt the third-party-MCP adaptation rules for wrapping other people's servers: pin a tool-catalog profile and fail closed, bind target identity by content hash not path, loopback-only endpoints with redirects refused, suppress inherited env, cap workers, never save/close/mutate state you did not create.

Bind every driven session to a stable target identity (document realpath, program SHA-256, document_generation counter, input hash + image base) and refuse when it changes, as each REA engine adapter does.

Avoid copying the full depth of REA's ownership machinery up front (Swift helper compilation, ps-based tables, ~2000-line ProcessOwnership.ts); start with Job Objects/cgroups + run tokens and the same fail-closed invariants, then grow.

Boundary flag: the Linux Hopper helper synthesizes clicks on the vendor's registration/demo dialog of a verified demo build; the downstream project should by policy exclude licensing, registration and consent dialogs from automatable UI to stay clearly inside 'software you own or are authorized to automate'.

Expect and design for partial cleanup under crashes (Windows job kill-on-close but residual files; upstream IDA workers outliving a killed supervisor; Kuna staging retained until stop is proven) by making 'incomplete' a first-class, retryable state rather than claiming success.
constraints_or_risks: Not a sandbox: the socket token protects the IPC channel, not the user account; any same-user process can read the private runtime, and engines, GDB/Rizin consoles and Frida scripts run with the user's full authority (SECURITY.md L33-36; docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md L43, L86).

Platform prerequisites for ownership proof: procps ps on Linux, Swift compiler via xcrun on macOS, and the packaged x64 native addon on Windows; persistent debugger sessions are Linux-only and Windows cannot host PTY capture (docs/ghidra-provider.md L10-11; docs/process-capture.md L19-40; native/windows/README.md).

Crash-time cleanup is best-effort: Windows kill-on-close guarantees process death but can leave private files; abruptly killed REA leaves IDA headless workers running; Kuna staging is retained until the stop is proven (docs/windows-ghidra-p0.md L238-239; docs/ida-provider.md L188; docs/kuna-provider.md L153).

Supply chain: REA itself is installed via npx -y rea-agents@<version>; it executes user-supplied Ghidra/JDK/IDA/JEB/Kuna/Frida binaries; Hopper Linux packages are verified only by HTTPS origin + vendor SHA-1 checksum; the IDA native plugin binds 0.0.0.0 and must be firewalled by the user (SECURITY.md L50; docs/ida-provider.md L60).

Licensing: IDA, JEB and Hopper are commercial; REA does not install, activate or license them and IDA Free decompilation requires cloud access and consent (docs/ida-provider.md L3, L78; docs/jeb-analysis.md L18); the Linux Hopper path automates the vendor demo dialog, which sits adjacent to the user's no-license-defeat boundary.

Resource control is partial: Ghidra heap via -Xmx only, no -max-cpu, JVM RSS and Node heap unbounded, OOM attribution not automatic; many caps (25 s Cutter request, 10 s GDB startup, 16 MiB outputs, 256 discovery candidates) have no runtime override (docs/installation.md L1579-1596; docs/ghidra-provider.md L27-31; docs/reverse-engineering-tools.md L43, L141-148).

UI side effects cannot be suppressed, only reported: IDA legacy proxy moves the GUI and closes pseudocode tabs; Hopper's macOS launcher may activate its window (docs/ida-provider.md L78, L149; src/hopper/BridgeLauncher.ts L181-194).

Complexity: the guarantees come with very large adapter surfaces (IdaSessionClient.ts 1046 lines, ProcessOwnership.ts 1956 lines, GhidraProviderClient.ts ~63 KB); distilling means extracting invariants, not porting code.
open_questions: How src/composition/binary.ts registers providers and whether a third-party provider can be added without modifying the package (plugin loading) -- outside this area.
Whether the Windows native addon is Authenticode-signed or only SHA-256/manifest-pinned by the npm package (README describes hash + manifest checks only).

Real behavior of macOS environment-withholding cases (platform binaries, restricted processes) when the owned process is a target GUI app rather than a REA helper; documented only as 'unverified' evidence.
Whether REA contains any accessibility-tree (AT-SPI/UIA/AX) automation; only X11 window-title matching plus XTest input was found in this checkout.
End-to-end behavior of Hopper bridge reconnection after a REA restart (bridge listen(1) with 30 s accept timeout vs HopperClient.#reconnectForCleanup) was not traced.
Exact Cutter plugin API surface relied upon (cutter.core().getConfig, cutter.cmd/cmdj) across Cutter versions; the docs label the bridge experimental.
